School Library

Start with a clean relational model of students, books, and loans. This worksheet covers relational database fundamentals, schema language, core retrieval queries, and a first step into DDL and DML.

Dataset

1

Schema Warm-Up

Use the table explorer, schema view, and ERD before writing queries.

  1. A3.1.1 Primary keys

    Name the three tables and identify the primary key in each one.

  2. A3.2.1 Schema levels

    State which schema level would show: the entities and their relationships, the data types and keys, and the indexing or storage choices.

  3. A3.1.1 Relationships

    Describe the relationship between STUDENT and LOAN, and between BOOK and LOAN. Include cardinality and the role of referential integrity.

  4. A3.1.1 Evaluation

2

Retrieve and Filter

Build confidence with SELECT, FROM, and WHERE.

Syntax reference — SELECT, WHERE, LIKE, BETWEEN 
-- Select all columns
SELECT * FROM table_name;

-- Select specific columns
SELECT col1, col2 FROM table_name;

-- Filter rows
SELECT * FROM table_name WHERE column = 'value';

-- AND / OR
SELECT * FROM table_name WHERE col1 = 'A' OR col1 = 'B';

-- BETWEEN (inclusive)
SELECT * FROM table_name WHERE year BETWEEN 2020 AND 2024;

-- LIKE with wildcards: % = any sequence of characters
--   Contains:    WHERE title LIKE '%Code%'
--   Starts with: WHERE title LIKE 'The%'
--   Ends with:   WHERE title LIKE '%ing'
SELECT title, author FROM BOOK WHERE title LIKE '%Code%';

SQL keywords are not case-sensitive, but it is convention to write them in UPPER CASE. String values in WHERE clauses are case-sensitive in most databases.

  1. A3.3.2 SELECT *

    Display every row and column from STUDENT.

  2. A3.3.2 Specific columns

    Show only FirstName, LastName, and TutorGroup for students in tutor group 12B.

  3. A3.3.2 AND / OR

    List the titles and genres of books where the genre is Science or Technology.

  4. A3.3.2 WHERE

    Find every loan record where ReturnStatus is Overdue.

  5. A3.3.2 BETWEEN

    Show books published between 2020 and 2024 inclusive.

  6. A3.3.2 LIKE

    Return the titles and authors of books whose title contains the word Code.

3

Sort the Result Set

Control how the rows are presented after filtering.

Syntax reference — ORDER BY, DISTINCT 
-- Sort ascending (A–Z, 0–9) — ASC is the default
SELECT * FROM table_name ORDER BY column ASC;

-- Sort descending (Z–A, 9–0)
SELECT * FROM table_name ORDER BY column DESC;

-- Sort by multiple columns (primary then secondary)
SELECT * FROM STUDENT ORDER BY TutorGroup ASC, LastName ASC;

-- DISTINCT removes duplicate values
SELECT DISTINCT ReturnStatus FROM LOAN ORDER BY ReturnStatus;

ORDER BY always applies to the final result set — put it at the end of your query, after any WHERE clause.

  1. A3.3.2 DISTINCT

    List every distinct value that appears in ReturnStatus, sorted alphabetically.

  2. A3.3.2 ORDER BY DESC

    Display book title, author, and published year, sorted newest to oldest. If two books share a year, sort those alphabetically by title.

  3. A3.3.2 ORDER BY ASC

    Show student names grouped by tutor group, then by last name.

4

First Joins

Use foreign keys to combine tables into one result set.

Syntax reference — JOIN 
-- INNER JOIN: only rows that match in both tables
SELECT col1, col2
FROM tableA
INNER JOIN tableB ON tableA.key = tableB.foreign_key;

-- Joining LOAN to STUDENT
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, l.ReturnStatus
FROM LOAN l
INNER JOIN STUDENT s ON l.StudentID = s.StudentID;

-- Joining three tables
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, b.Title, l.DueDate
FROM LOAN l
INNER JOIN STUDENT s ON l.StudentID = s.StudentID
INNER JOIN BOOK b   ON l.BookID    = b.BookID
WHERE l.ReturnStatus = 'On Loan'
ORDER BY l.DueDate;

Use table aliases (e.g. l, s, b) to keep long queries readable. Always qualify column names with the alias when the same column name exists in more than one table.

  1. A3.3.2 JOIN 2 tables

    Join LOAN to STUDENT and show which students currently have a book On Loan.

  2. A3.3.2 JOIN 2 tables

    Join LOAN to BOOK to list the titles, authors, and due dates for every overdue loan.

  3. A3.3.2 JOIN 3 tables

    Show each current loan with student full name, book title, author, and due date. Sort by due date first.

  4. A3.1.1 Integrity

    Explain why a loan row with StudentID = 9999 should be rejected in a relational database with referential integrity turned on.

5

DDL and DML

Complete these last. They change the live workspace.

Syntax reference — CREATE TABLE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE 
-- Create a table (DDL)
CREATE TABLE REVIEW (
    ReviewID   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    BookID     INTEGER,
    Rating     INTEGER,
    Comment    TEXT,
    FOREIGN KEY (BookID) REFERENCES BOOK(BookID)
);

-- Insert a row (DML)
INSERT INTO REVIEW (ReviewID, BookID, Rating, Comment)
VALUES (1, 2002, 5, 'Excellent introduction to coding.');

-- Update a row (DML) — always include a WHERE clause
UPDATE LOAN
SET ReturnStatus = 'Returned'
WHERE LoanID = 3006;

-- Delete a row (DML) — always include a WHERE clause
DELETE FROM REVIEW
WHERE ReviewID = 1;

DDL (Data Definition Language) changes the structure — CREATE, ALTER, DROP. DML (Data Manipulation Language) changes the data — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT.

  1. A3.3.1 DDL

    Create a new table called REVIEW with columns ReviewID, BookID, Rating, and Comment. Make ReviewID the primary key and link BookID back to BOOK.

  2. A3.3.3 INSERT

    Insert one review for BookID 2002 with a rating and a short comment.

  3. A3.3.3 UPDATE

    Update loan 3006 so that its ReturnStatus becomes Returned.

  4. A3.3.3 DELETE

    Delete the review row you added, then check that the table is empty again.

Model Answers — School Library

Section 1 — Schema Warm-Up

1
Three tables and primary keys STUDENT → StudentID  |  BOOK → BookID  |  LOAN → LoanID
2
Schema levels Entities and relationships → conceptual schema (ERD). Data types and keys → logical schema. Indexing and storage → physical schema.
3
Relationships STUDENT to LOAN: one-to-many (one student can have many loans; each loan belongs to exactly one student). BOOK to LOAN: one-to-many (one book can appear in many loan records). Referential integrity ensures a StudentID or BookID in LOAN must exist in the parent table.
4
Benefit / Limitation Benefit: data is stored once and linked, avoiding duplication (e.g. a student's name is in one place). Limitation: queries across tables require joins, which adds complexity compared to a single flat spreadsheet.

Section 2 — Retrieve and Filter

1 
SELECT * FROM STUDENT;
2 
SELECT FirstName, LastName, TutorGroup
FROM STUDENT
WHERE TutorGroup = '12B';
3 
SELECT Title, Genre
FROM BOOK
WHERE Genre = 'Science' OR Genre = 'Technology';
4 
SELECT * FROM LOAN
WHERE ReturnStatus = 'Overdue';
5 
SELECT * FROM BOOK
WHERE PublishedYear BETWEEN 2020 AND 2024;
6 
SELECT Title, Author
FROM BOOK
WHERE Title LIKE '%Code%';

Section 3 — Sort the Result Set

1 
SELECT DISTINCT ReturnStatus
FROM LOAN
ORDER BY ReturnStatus;
2 
SELECT Title, Author, PublishedYear
FROM BOOK
ORDER BY PublishedYear DESC, Title ASC;
3 
SELECT FirstName, LastName, TutorGroup
FROM STUDENT
ORDER BY TutorGroup ASC, LastName ASC;

Section 4 — First Joins

1 
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName
FROM LOAN l
INNER JOIN STUDENT s ON l.StudentID = s.StudentID
WHERE l.ReturnStatus = 'On Loan';
2 
SELECT b.Title, b.Author, l.DueDate
FROM LOAN l
INNER JOIN BOOK b ON l.BookID = b.BookID
WHERE l.ReturnStatus = 'Overdue';
3 
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, b.Title, b.Author, l.DueDate
FROM LOAN l
INNER JOIN STUDENT s ON l.StudentID = s.StudentID
INNER JOIN BOOK b   ON l.BookID    = b.BookID
WHERE l.ReturnStatus = 'On Loan'
ORDER BY l.DueDate;
4
Referential integrity The LOAN table has a foreign key on StudentID that references STUDENT(StudentID). If StudentID = 9999 does not exist in STUDENT, the database engine refuses the insert to maintain referential integrity — preventing orphaned loan records that cannot be linked to a real student.

Section 5 — DDL and DML

1 
CREATE TABLE REVIEW (
    ReviewID  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    BookID    INTEGER,
    Rating    INTEGER,
    Comment   TEXT,
    FOREIGN KEY (BookID) REFERENCES BOOK(BookID)
);
2 
INSERT INTO REVIEW (ReviewID, BookID, Rating, Comment)
VALUES (1, 2002, 5, 'A brilliant read.');
3 
UPDATE LOAN
SET ReturnStatus = 'Returned'
WHERE LoanID = 3006;
4 
DELETE FROM REVIEW WHERE ReviewID = 1;
SELECT * FROM REVIEW; -- should return 0 rows
